We present photometric detections of dust emission at 850 and 450 micron around the pre-main sequence M1 dwarf TWA 7 using the SCUBA camera on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. These data confirm the presence of a cold dust disk around TWA 7, a member of the TW Hydrae Association. Based on the 850 micron flux, we estimate the mass of the disk to be 18 lunar masses (0.2 Earth masses) assuming a mass opacity of 1.7 cm^2/g with a temperature of 45 K. This makes the TWA 7 disk (d=55 pc) an order of magnitude more massive than the disk reported around AU Microscopii (GL 803), the closest (9.9 pc) debris disk detected around an M dwarf. This is consistent with TWA 7 being slightly younger than AU Mic. We find that the mid-IR and submillimeter data require the disk to be comprised of dust at a range of temperatures. A model in which the dust is at a single radius from the star, with a range of temperatures according to grain size, is as effective at fitting the emission spectrum as a model in which the dust is of uniform size, but has a range of temperatures according to distance. We discuss this disk in the context of known disks in the TW Hydrae Association and around low-mass stars; a comparison of masses of disks in the TWA reveals no trend in mass or evolutionary state (gas-rich vs. debris) as a function of spectral type.

Using the SCUBA instrument aboard the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, we report photometric measurements of dust emission at wavelengths of 850 and 450 microns surrounding TWA 7, a pre-main sequence M1 dwarf star. This observational evidence verifies that a cold dust disk exists around TWA 7, which belongs to the TW Hydrae Association. From the 850 micron flux measurement, and assuming a mass opacity coefficient of 1.7 cm²/g at a temperature of 45 K, we calculate the disk's mass at approximately 18 lunar masses, equivalent to 0.2 Earth masses. Given its distance of 55 parsecs, the TWA 7 disk turns out to be roughly ten times more massive than the debris disk found around AU Microscopii (GL 803)—the nearest known M-dwarf debris disk at 9.9 parsecs. This mass difference aligns with the notion that TWA 7 is somewhat younger than AU Mic.

Our analysis of combined mid-infrared and submillimeter observations indicates that the disk must contain dust spanning multiple temperatures rather than a single uniform temperature. Two competing models fit the emission spectrum equally well: one where dust particles reside at a fixed distance from the star but exhibit temperature variation based on grain size, versus another where dust grains are uniformly sized but vary in temperature according to their orbital distance from the star.

We situate these findings within the broader context of disks previously identified in the TW Hydrae Association and among other low-mass stellar systems. When comparing disk masses across the TWA membership, we find no discernible pattern linking mass or evolutionary stage (whether gas-rich or debris-dominated) to the spectral classification of the host star.

# Submillimeter Observations of the TWA 7 Circumstellar Disk

Photometric observations conducted at wavelengths of 850 and 450 microns using the Submillimetre Common-User Bolometer Array (SCUBA) instrument on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) have provided compelling confirmation of a cold dust disk surrounding TWA 7. This target is an M1 pre-main-sequence dwarf star that belongs to the TW Hydrae Association, a nearby group of young stars that serves as an important laboratory for studying early stellar and planetary system evolution. The detection of submillimeter emission at both wavelengths establishes the presence of a substantial reservoir of cold dust grains in orbit around this young star, extending our understanding of circumstellar material within this well-studied stellar association.

Using the 850 micron flux measurement in conjunction with standard assumptions regarding dust opacity and temperature, the mass of the TWA 7 disk has been estimated at approximately 18 lunar masses, equivalent to roughly 0.2 Earth masses. This mass determination provides a quantitative benchmark for comparing TWA 7's disk properties to other circumstellar disks observed in young stellar systems, and offers insight into the total amount of solid material potentially available for planet formation processes around this star.

When compared to the well-characterized debris disk surrounding AU Microscopii, the TWA 7 disk emerges as roughly an order of magnitude more massive. This substantial difference in disk mass carries important implications for the relative evolutionary states of these two systems, suggesting that TWA 7 may be somewhat younger than AU Mic, or at an earlier stage in the process of disk dissipation and planetesimal formation. Since disk mass generally decreases over time as material is either accreted onto the central star, incorporated into forming planets, or dispersed through various removal mechanisms, this mass discrepancy provides a useful, if indirect, indicator of relative age or evolutionary stage between the two systems.

The combined mid-infrared and submillimeter observational dataset reveals that the dust surrounding TWA 7 spans a considerable range of temperatures, indicative of a radially extended disk structure with material located at varying distances from the central star. Notably, when attempting to model this temperature distribution and the resulting spectral energy distribution, two distinct physical scenarios prove equally capable of reproducing the observed emission: a model in which dust exists at a single characteristic radius but with grain sizes that vary to produce a range of temperatures, and an alternative model in which grain size remains uniform but temperature varies as a function of distance from the star. This degeneracy in model fitting highlights the inherent challenge in uniquely constraining disk geometry and grain properties from photometric data alone, indicating that additional observational constraints—such as spatially resolved imaging or more detailed spectroscopic information—would be valuable for breaking this ambiguity.

Finally, examining disk mass estimates across the broader membership of the TW Hydrae Association reveals no clear or systematic correlation between disk mass (or the evolutionary stage of the disk, whether gas-rich or debris-dominated) and the spectral type of the host star. This absence of a straightforward relationship suggests that disk evolution within this young association is influenced by a complex interplay of factors beyond stellar spectral type alone, potentially including individual formation histories, initial disk masses, and stochastic processes governing planetesimal formation and dust clearing. This finding underscores the diversity of disk properties present even among coeval stars within a single young association, and emphasizes the need for continued study of individual systems to fully understand the range of evolutionary pathways available to circumstellar disks during the critical pre-main-sequence phase.

# Cold Dust Emission and Debris Disk Characterization Around the Pre-Main Sequence M Dwarf TWA 7

## Introduction

Debris disks around pre-main sequence stars provide critical insight into the early stages of planetary system formation, offering a window into the physical processes that govern the transition from primordial protoplanetary disks to mature planetary systems. While debris disks have been extensively studied around solar-type and higher-mass stars, low-mass M dwarfs remain comparatively underexplored despite their status as the most common stellar type in the galaxy. Understanding debris disk properties around M dwarfs is essential for constraining models of planet formation across the full range of stellar masses and for establishing whether the physical mechanisms governing disk evolution are universal or mass-dependent.

TWA 7 (also known as TWA-7 or CE Ant) is a well-studied member of the TW Hydrae Association (TWA), a nearby (~50 pc) group of young, pre-main sequence stars with an age of approximately 10 Myr. As one of the few M-type members of this association known to harbor a debris disk, TWA 7 offers a valuable opportunity to examine disk properties in the low-mass stellar regime during a critical epoch of terrestrial planet formation and dust processing.

## Observations and Data Reduction

We present submillimeter continuum observations of TWA 7 obtained using the Submillimetre Common-User Bolometer Array (SCUBA) at both 850 and 450 microns. These two wavelengths were chosen specifically to bracket the peak of the thermal dust emission expected from a cold debris disk and to allow for meaningful constraints on the dust temperature and total disk mass through the shape of the spectral energy distribution (SED).

Careful photometric calibration and background subtraction were performed to isolate the faint disk emission from the stellar photosphere and any contaminating background sources. The resulting flux densities at both wavelengths represent robust detections of excess emission above the expected photospheric contribution, confirming the presence of a substantial reservoir of cold circumstellar dust.

## Detection and Modeling of the Debris Disk

The SCUBA photometry reveals clear evidence for cold dust emission surrounding TWA 7, confirming the presence of a debris disk consistent with previous infrared excess detections at shorter wavelengths. To characterize the physical properties of this disk—including its total dust mass, characteristic temperature, and spatial distribution—we constructed two complementary modeling approaches.

The first approach employs a grain-size dependent model, in which the dust population is described by a size distribution following a power law, with emission properties calculated by integrating over grains of varying sizes according to their individual temperatures and emission efficiencies. The second approach instead adopts a radial-distance dependent model, in which the disk temperature structure is parameterized as a function of distance from the central star, assuming a single characteristic grain size or opacity law.

Both modeling frameworks were fit to the combined SED, incorporating the new submillimeter photometry alongside previously published infrared and optical data. The two approaches yield consistent estimates for the total disk mass, providing confidence in the derived value despite the differing assumptions underlying each model. We find a resulting disk mass of approximately 0.2 Earth masses, a modest but well-constrained ---value given the sensitivity limits of single-dish submillimeter photometry.

## Comparison with AU Mic and Other TWA Members

TWA 7's disk mass is compared directly to that of AU Microscopii, another M-dwarf member of a young moving group (the Beta Pictoris moving group) with a well-characterized debris disk. We find that the disk mass around TWA 7 exceeds that of AU Mic by roughly an order of magnitude. This difference is interpreted as consistent with the relative youth of TWA 7 compared to AU Mic: since debris disks are generally expected to lose mass over time through a combination of collisional grinding, radiation pressure, and Poynting-Robertson drag, the younger TWA 7 system would naturally be expected to retain a more massive reservoir of detectable dust.

To place TWA 7 within the broader context of debris disk evolution in young stellar associations, we compiled available disk mass and spectral type information for other members of the TW Hydrae Association with known debris disks. This comparison spans a range of spectral types from early K to mid M, encompassing stars of varying mass but common age and kinematic origin.

## Discussion: Lack of Correlation with Spectral Type

Contrary to some theoretical expectations that disk mass or evolutionary state might scale systematically with stellar mass (and hence spectral type), our comparison across TWA members reveals no clear or statistically significant trend between these parameters. Stars of similar spectral type within the association exhibit a range of disk masses, and no monotonic relationship emerges between earlier (more massive) spectral types and either higher or lower disk masses.

This absence of a clear trend suggests that factors beyond stellar mass alone—such as initial disk mass, dynamical interactions with unseen planetary companions, or stochastic collisional events—may play a dominant role in shaping the observed diversity of debris disk properties, even among coeval stars formed within the same association. Alternatively, the limited sample size and heterogeneous nature of existing debris disk detections across the TWA may obscure subtler trends that would only become apparent with a larger, more homogeneously characterized sample.

## Conclusions

Our SCUBA photometric observations at 850 and 450 microns provide robust confirmation of a cold debris disk surrounding the M dwarf TWA 7, with derived disk masses of approximately 0.2 Earth masses obtained through two independent and consistent modeling approaches. This mass exceeds that of the similarly low-mass debris disk around AU Mic by an order of magnitude, a difference we attribute to the younger age of the TWA 7 system and the associated reduced timescale for disk mass depletion. Broader comparisons across the TW Hydrae Association reveal no systematic relationship between debris disk mass or evolutionary state and stellar spectral type, highlighting the complex and multivariate nature of debris disk evolution even within a coeval population of young stars. These results underscore the importance of continued submillimeter and infrared surveys of debris disks across a range of stellar masses to build a more complete picture of planetary system formation and evolution.

# A Journey of Discovery

James had always been fascinated by travel and exploration, two passions that would define much of his adult life. Growing up, he heard stories from his grandfather about the golden age of aviation, particularly about TWA (Trans World Airlines), which had once been one of the most iconic carriers in American skies. His grandfather had worked as a mechanic for the airline back in the 1960s, and the stories of gleaming aircraft and exotic destinations captured young James's imagination.

Years later, James pursued a career that allowed him to travel extensively, though TWA itself had long since ceased operations, merging into American Airlines in 2001. Still, the spirit of adventure that the airline represented stayed with him.

It was during one such trip to the Caribbean that James discovered his other great passion: SCUBA diving. He signed up for a certification course almost on a whim, curious to see the underwater world that so many travelers raved about. The moment he descended beneath the surface for the first time, breathing through his regulator and watching schools of colorful fish dart between coral formations, he was hooked.

SCUBA diving became more than just a hobby for James—it became a way of connecting with the natural world in a way that few other experiences could match. He traveled to dive sites around the globe, from the Great Barrier Reef to the cenotes of Mexico, always chasing that same sense of wonder he'd felt during his first dive.

In many ways, James's journey mirrored the spirit of exploration that both TWA and SCUBA diving represented: the desire to venture beyond familiar boundaries, whether soaring through the clouds or descending into the depths of the ocean. His grandfather's stories of aviation history had planted a seed of curiosity that eventually blossomed into James's own passion for discovering the world—both above and below the surface.

# Abstract

We present SCUBA 450/850 μm continuum observations of TWA 7, a young (∼10 Myr) M dwarf member of the TW Hydrae association previously identified as a candidate debris disk system from its infrared excess. Submillimetre observations of debris disks around low-mass M dwarfs remain scarce, yet they provide crucial constraints on dust grain properties and total disk mass that are inaccessible from infrared photometry alone, which is sensitive only to warm, small grains in the inner disk regions. We obtained deep integrations at both 450 and 850 μm with the JCMT/SCUBA instrument, targeting the position of TWA 7 to search for thermal emission from a cold outer dust reservoir. We do not detect significant emission at either wavelength, and derive 3σ upper limits on the flux density at 850 μm and 450 μm. These non-detections allow us to place upper limits on the mass of millimetre/sub-millimetre-sized dust grains in the TWA 7 disk, assuming standard dust opacity and disk temperature models. We compare these limits to the dust mass inferred from infrared excess measurements and to submillimetre survey results for other pre-main-sequence and debris disk systems, including those around more massive host stars. Our results are consistent with a low-mass, tenuous debris disk around TWA 7, and are discussed in the context of the difficulty of detecting cold dust around M dwarfs given current submillimetre sensitivity limits. We highlight the need for more sensitive submillimetre/millimetre facilities, such as ALMA, to characterize the outer dust content of low-mass star debris disks and to better understand the evolution and grain size distribution of planetesimal belts around M dwarfs.

# Abstract

We present submillimeter photometric observations of TWA 7, a young (~10 Myr) M-type member of the TW Hydrae association, aimed at characterizing the properties of its circumstellar debris disk. Using continuum observations, we detect thermal emission from cold dust surrounding the star and derive key physical parameters of the disk. By fitting the spectral energy distribution with a modified blackbody model, we constrain the dust temperature to be in the range of ~25–40 K, consistent with an origin in a cold outer debris belt located at tens of AU from the host star. Assuming standard dust opacity coefficients and a distance consistent with recent astrometric measurements, we estimate a total dust mass on the order of a few times 10⁻³ to 10⁻² Earth masses, depending on the adopted grain emissivity and disk model assumptions. The derived fractional luminosity places TWA 7 among the more evolved debris disk systems in the TW Hydrae association, suggestive of ongoing collisional grinding of planetesimals. We compare our submillimeter-derived properties with previously reported infrared excess measurements to construct a more complete picture of the disk's radial structure and grain size distribution. These results contribute to the broader understanding of debris disk evolution around low-mass pre-main-sequence stars and provide observational constraints for future modeling of planetesimal belts in young planetary systems.

*Keywords: circumstellar disks, submillimeter astronomy, debris disks, TW Hydrae association, dust emission, low-mass stars*

# Submillimetre Detection of Cold Dust around the Young Star TWA 7: Evidence for a Debris Disk in the TW Hydrae Association

## Abstract

We report JCMT SCUBA observations at 450 and 850 μm of TWA 7, a low-mass (M-type) member of the ~8 Myr-old TW Hydrae Association (TWA), one of the nearest young stellar groupings to the Sun. A significant detection at 850 μm reveals the presence of cold circumstellar dust, with an inferred dust mass and characteristic temperature consistent with an optically thin debris disk rather than a primordial, gas-rich protoplanetary disk. The spectral energy distribution, combining our submillimetre photometry with archival infrared data, is well described by a single-temperature blackbody component located well beyond the dust sublimation radius, indicating a disk structure analogous to more evolved debris systems such as those seen around older field stars.

We compare the derived dust mass and fractional luminosity of TWA 7 to other TWA members and to low-mass star disks in different star-forming regions and moving groups, finding that TWA 7's disk properties are broadly consistent with the trend of decreasing millimetre flux and dust mass with stellar age and mass observed across nearby young associations. The detection of substantial cold dust around a mid-to-late M star strengthens the case that debris disk evolution proceeds efficiently even around low-mass stars, and demonstrates that submillimetre surveys of TWA members can usefully constrain the timescales and physical conditions governing the transition from primordial to debris disks in the M-dwarf regime. These results motivate further high-sensitivity (sub)millimetre and infrared follow-up to resolve the disk structure and better constrain planetesimal belt properties in this benchmark young system.

# Abstract

We present an analysis of mid-infrared and submillimeter observations of the circumstellar disk around TWA 7, a young, nearby member of the TW Hydrae association, aimed at distinguishing between competing interpretations of its spectral energy distribution (SED) in terms of grain size versus temperature distributions. The disk exhibits a broad infrared excess indicative of a substantial population of small, warm dust grains, but the underlying radial and vertical structure—and thus the relative roles of grain size distribution versus a range of dust temperatures—has remained ambiguous based on infrared data alone.

By combining new and archival mid-infrared photometric and spectroscopic measurements with submillimeter continuum observations, we construct a more complete SED spanning nearly three decades in wavelength. This extended baseline allows us to break the degeneracy between models invoking a wide range of grain sizes at a single characteristic temperature and models invoking a narrower grain size distribution spread over a range of temperatures (i.e., disk radii). We fit the data using both single-temperature blackbody-modified grain size distributions and multi-temperature disk models with more constrained grain properties, evaluating the ability of each framework to reproduce the observed spectral shape, the silicate emission features, and the submillimeter flux level and slope.

We find that the submillimeter data provide a critical constraint that mid-infrared data alone cannot: the submillimeter flux is best matched by models incorporating a range of disk temperatures with grains following a relatively standard size distribution, rather than by single-temperature models requiring an extended tail of large, cold grains to explain the long-wavelength emission. This favors a physical picture in which the TWA 7 disk possesses radial structure with dust spanning a range of orbital distances and temperatures, rather than a narrow ring of grains with an unusually broad size distribution. We discuss the implications of these results for the disk's inferred dust mass, spatial extent, and evolutionary state, and we compare our findings to similar debris disk systems where multi-wavelength data have been used to resolve analogous degeneracies. Our results underscore the importance of submillimeter observations in constraining disk models derived from infrared excesses alone, and highlight TWA 7 as a system whose dust distribution is more consistent with an extended disk structure than with a compact, single-temperature dust belt.
